newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin seeks Maskhadov meeting despite strains.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin seeks Maskhadov meeting despite strains.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday reaffirmed his wish to meet Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov in the near future but a senior Chechen official accused the Russian military of trying to sabotage the meeting.

Russian news agencies quoted Yeltsin as saying Moscow must fulfil all its obligations under agreements it has signed with the breakaway region, including the release of funds to help rebuild Chechnya's shattered economy and infrastructure.
"We have to fulfil what we promised," RIA Novosti news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying during a meeting in the Kremlin with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
"Otherwise extremists (in Chechnya) criticise Maskhadov," the president added.
The two sides have still not agreed on a date or venue for the meeting but Kremlin sources said it was likely to take place on Friday or Saturday.
The sources also said Moscow had rejected Chechen suggestions that the meeting take place in a neutral location like Azerbaijan or Belarus.
However Chechnya's First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov said the meeting might not happen at all due to what he called "provocation" by the Russian military.

Udugov, who had been due to come to Moscow on Wednesday or Thursday to prepare the meeting, was referring to an incident on Wednesday in which an aircraft fired flares over the Chechen capital Grozny.
"This act by the Russian military is viewed as a provocation aimed at disrupting the meeting of the presidents of Russia and Chechnya," Interfax news agency quoted Udugov as saying.

However, in a bizarre twist, sources in Chechnya's Interior Ministry told Reuters the plane was actually Chechen and that it had been rehearsing for a parade to mark the republic's Independence Day on September 6.
Russian Air Force officials told Interfax they had no information of any Russian planes flying over Grozny and said they were surprised by Udugov's remarks.

The incident revealed the still widespread jitters in Chechnya about Russia's intentions a year after the two sides signed a peace pact ending their bloody 21-month conflict in which tens of thousands of people were killed.
Talks aimed at normalising relations between Moscow and Grozny are stalled over the vexed issue of Chechnya's status.
Maskhadov, buoyed by the separatists' battlefield victory, insists that his republic is fully independent but Yeltsin wants Chechnya to remain loosely within the Russian Federation.
